solution.explanation: Answer d – Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 591

question: Which PDE5 inhibitor has an overall lower risk of side effects, including penile pain and priapism?

solution.explanation: Answer d – Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 591

question: Posterior urethral valves are more common in children with which condition?

solution.explanation: Answer c – Incidence is One in >5000 ♂ (higher in Down’s syndrome). Pathology - PUV may arise through an abnormal insertion of the Wolffian ducts into the urogenital sinus around week 7 of fetal development. Presentation-Prenatal USS: 80% are diagnosed prenatally, with 60% identified on USS at 20wk. Immediate referral to specialist centres after birth is recommended. PUV account for 1% of cases of antenatal hydronephrosis. Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 704

question: VURD syndrome in the context of PUV refers to:
options: Bilateral reflux with normal renal function
Unilateral reflux into a non-functioning dysplastic kidney

solution.explanation: Answer b – pop- off valve syndrome’ is seen in 20% of PUV. It describes mechanisms by which high urinary tract pressure is dissipated to allow normal renal development. It includes leaking of urine from a small bladder or renal pelvis rupture (urinary ascites), unilateral reflux into a non- functioning kidney (VUR with renal dysplasia or VURD), and formation of bladder diverticuli. Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 704

question: Spontaneous resolution of hydronephrosis in PUJO occurs in approximately:?

solution.explanation: Answer c – Long- term studies in patients with good renal function have demonstrated that function frequently remains stable (56%) or spontaneous resolution occurs (27%), with only 17% requiring pyeloplasty for loss of function.1 The likelihood of requiring surgery is higher with greater TAPD: <20mm, 3% re- quire surgery; 20– 29mm, 20% surgery; 30– 39mm, 50% surgery; 40– 49mm, 80% surgery; and >50mm, up to 100% surgery.2 Overall, 90% of patients with a TAPD of >30mm will require surgery.  Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 703

question: Which of the following is a key pathophysiological factor in nocturnal enuresis?

solution.explanation: Answer c – Pathophysiology -Three main factors that interact to produce NE are: Altered ADH secretion: an abnormal decrease in ADH levels at night causes i urine production (NP). Altered sleep/ arousal mechanism: impaired ‘arousal from sleep’ response to a full bladder. Reduced nocturnal functional bladder capacity (± nocturnal detrusor overactivity). Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 724

question: Which antimuscarinic agent has a mixed mechanism of action, including antimuscarinic, local anaesthetic, and direct smooth muscle relaxation effects?

solution.explanation: Answer e – Oxybutynin: mixed action (antimuscarinic, LA, and direct muscle relaxation). It is available as immediate- or extended- release (er) tablets, transdermal patch and gel preparations, and can be given intravesically. It is effective but has a high rate of side effects, reducing patient compliance. NICE recommends this as a first- line drug treatment. Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 162

question: Which antimuscarinic is highly selective for M3 receptors?

solution.explanation: Answer d – Darifenacin: highly selective M3 antagonist. Achieves significant reduction in urinary frequency, urgency, incontinence episodes (77% with 15mg dose).It is well tolerated (2.1% discontinued 15mg treatment due to side effects). NICE recommends this as a first- line drug treatment. Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 162

question: Sipuleucel-T showed benefit specifically in men with:

solution.explanation: Answer b – Provenge® (sipuleucel- T) vaccine: this is the first patient- derived US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved CRPC immunotherapy against prostatic acid phosphatase. A 4- month survival advantage has been demonstrated over placebo in a randomized trial of men with minimally symptomatic CRPC (IMPACT, 2010). Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 377

question: Sipuleucel-T targets which prostate cancer antigen?

solution.explanation: Answer c – Provenge® (sipuleucel- T) vaccine: this is the first patient- derived US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved CRPC immunotherapy against prostatic acid phosphatase. A 4- month survival advantage has been demonstrated over placebo in a randomized trial of men with minimally symptomatic CRPC (IMPACT, 2010). Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 377

question: Radium-223 (Alpharadin) primarily benefits patients with CRPC by:
options: Reducing bone skeletal-related events and pain

solution.explanation: Answer c – Radium- 223 (Alpharadin): reduced bone SREs, bone pain, and prolonged survival by 3.6 months in a UK placebo- controlled RCT of 922 CRPC patients (ALSYMPCA, 2013). It is approved for use by UK NICE, either post- docetaxel or in CRPC patients unsuitable to receive docetaxel. Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 377

question: A patient with suspected CIS undergoes enhanced cystoscopy using blue light after intravesical instillation of hexaminolevulinic acid. The abnormal areas fluoresce red. What is the underlying mechanism?
options: Accumulation of porphyrin IX in cancer cells

solution.explanation: Answer b – PDD (fluorescence cystoscopy): uses blue light (400nm) in combination with an intravesical porphyrin- based photosensitizer hexaminolevulinic acid (HAL). In bladder cancer cells, this leads to red fluorescence (640nm) due to high levels of the heme intermediate protoporphyrin IX. Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 293

question: Which extrarenal cystic manifestation is most common in ADPKD?

solution.explanation: Answer d – The kidneys reach an enormous size due to multiple fluid- filled cysts and can easily be palpated on abdominal examination. Expansion of the cysts results in ischaemic atrophy of the surrounding renal parenchyma and obstruction of normal renal tubules. End- stage renal failure occurs at around age 50y. Associated disorders Ten to 30% incidence of circle of Willis berry aneurysms (associated with subarachnoid haemorrhage), cysts of the liver (33%), pancreas (10%), spleen (<5%), and seminal vesicles, mitral valve prolapse, aortic root dila- tation, aortic aneurysms, and diverticular disease. Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 416

question: Regarding malignancy risk in ADPKD, which statement is correct?
options: RCC risk is lower than the general population
RCC risk is the same as the general population
RCC is the leading cause of death

solution.explanation: Answer c – Of note, the incidence of renal adenoma is 720%; however, the risk of RCC is the same as the general population. Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 416

question: A woman with non-obstructive urinary retention undergoes SNS implantation. What proportion of such patients no longer require intermittent self-catheterisation (ISC) at 18 months?

solution.explanation: Answer d – For non- obstructive urinary retention in those responding to PNE and who were subsequently implanted, 58% no longer re- quired ISC at 18 months of follow- up,7 results mirrored by others (50– 55% stopping ISC) at a mean of 41– 43 months (70% with Fowler’s syndrome) Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 655

question: Which subgroup of patients with urinary retention has the highest response rate to Sacral neuromodulation, with around 70% stopping ISC?

solution.explanation: Answer d – Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 655

question: A 29-year-old primigravida is reviewed at 16 weeks’ gestation. She is asymptomatic and has normal blood pressure and urine analysis. Which of the following best describes the change in renal plasma flow (RPF) during normal pregnancy?
options: It decreases progressively from the first trimester
It increases by approximately 25% by 16 weeks and returns to normal by term
It increases early, rising by about 75% by 16 weeks and is maintained until late pregnancy
It remains unchanged until the third trimester
It peaks in the third trimester and remains elevated postpartum

solution.explanation: Answer c – Renal plasma flow (RPF) rate: goes up early in the first trimester, reaching an increase of 75% by 16wk gestation. This is maintained until 34wk gestation, followed by a decline of 25% towards term. The question can be asked on GFR as well – in that case remember this from Oxford - The GFR: increases by 50% by the end of the first trimester, which is maintained until term. GFR has returned to normal levels by 3 months after delivery. Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 658

question: What is the approximate radiation dose of a standard CT-KUB ?

solution.explanation: Answer d – CT- KUB radiation dose: 74.7mSv, compared to 1.5mSv for IVU (fatal cancer risk is estimated at 1 in 2000 for a 10mSv radiation exposure). ULDCT lowers radiation exposure (0.6– 2mSv), but at the expense of a lower sensitivity (68– 86%) for small (<3mm) ureteric stones. CEULDCT uses contrast which increases sensitivity (97%) and specificity (100%) for detecting small ureteric stone disease, while limiting radiation dose to levels comparable with IVU (1.7mSv vs 1.4mSv). Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 478

question: A 32-year-old man presents with acute flank pain suggestive of ureteric colic. Which statement best compares standard CT-KUB and ultra-low-dose CT (ULDCT) ?
options: Standard CT-KUB has a radiation dose similar to IVU but lower sensitivity
ULDCT has higher sensitivity than standard CT-KUB for small stones
Standard CT-KUB has a higher radiation dose but has greater sensitivity than ULDCT
ULDCT delivers higher radiation than standard CT-KUB but avoids contrast use
Both have equivalent radiation dose and sensitivity

solution.explanation: Answer c – CT- KUB radiation dose: 4.7mSv, compared to 1.5mSv for IVU (fatal cancer risk is estimated at 1 in 2000 for a 10mSv radiation exposure). ULDCT lowers radiation exposure (0.6– 2mSv), but at the expense of a lower sensitivity (68– 86%) for small (<3mm) ureteric stones. CEULDCT uses contrast which increases sensitivity (97%) and specificity (100%) for detecting small ureteric stone disease, while limiting radiation dose to levels comparable with IVU (1.7mSv vs 1.4mSv). Oxford handbook of Urology Page- 478

question: A 45-year-old man undergoes renal transplantation and is commenced on tacrolimus. What is its primary mechanism of action?

solution.explanation: Answer c – Tacrolimus inhibits T lymphocyte activation by binding to FKBP-12, an intracellular protein. A complex is then formed of tacrolimus–FKBP-12, calcium, calmodulin, and calcineurin, which inhibits the phosphatase activity of calcineurin. Peter Morris Page - 243

question: Which histological finding is characteristic of AMR on renal transplant biopsy?

solution.explanation: Answer c – The diagnosis of AMR is based on the presence of DSA in recipient serum and biopsy of the transplanted kidney demonstrating microvascular inflammation (glomerulitis or peritubular capillaritis), immune cell infiltration, and usually evidence of complement activation by C4d staining of peritubular capillaries. Peter Morris Page - 204

question: Most common location of post-transplant lymphoceles are :
options: Adjacent to the upper pole of the kidney
Adjacent to the lower pole of the kidney

solution.explanation: Answer c – Larger collections may become apparent clinically and usually do so at 1 week to 6 months after transplantation, with a peak incidence after hospital dis- charge toward the end of the first month. Most are situated adjacent to the lower pole of the kidney and posterolateral to the transplant ureter. Although intralymphocele fluid pressure measurements have not been reported, they must be considerable. The most common presentation is sleep disturbance owing to urinary frequency as a result of compression of the bladder. Peter Morris Page - 480

question: Which statement best describes universal CMV prophylaxis after transplantation?
options: Antivirals only after positive CMV PCR
Antivirals given to all at-risk patients for a defined period
Reserved for CMV Reactive− recipients only

solution.explanation: Answer b – Two strategies are commonly used for CMV prevention—universal prophylaxis and preemptive therapy. Universal prophylaxis involves giving antiviral therapy to all at-risk patients after transplantation for a defined period. In preemptive therapy, QNAT assays are used to monitor patients at predefined intervals (generally weekly for weeks 1–12) to detect early disease. Prophylaxis has the possible advantage of not only preventing CMV infection during the period of greatest risk but also diminishing infections secondary to HHV-6, HHV-7, and EBV. In practice, neither universal prophylaxis nor preemptive therapy is perfect. Many centers use a combination of both approaches: universal prophylaxis for the highest-risk recipients (Donor+/Recipient− and Recipient+ with T cell depletion) and preemptive therapy for others. Peter Morris Page – 528

question: According to UK standards, permanent vascular access for dialysis should ideally be constructed how long before the anticipated need for dialysis?
options: At the time of dialysis initiation

solution.explanation: Answer d – In the UK the Renal Association and the joint working party of the Renal Association, the Vascular Society of Great Britain and Ireland, and the British Society of Interventional Radiology have produced the following standards:  65% of all patients presenting within 3 months of dialysis should start hemodialysis on a useable AVF. • 85% of all prevalent hemodialysis patients should be dialyzed using a native AVF. □ No patient requiring dialysis should wait more than 4 weeks for fistula construction. □ Permanent access should be constructed 16 weeks and preferably 6 months before anticipated need for dialysis. □ Preservation of arm veins is critical and unnecessary venipuncture must be avoided. Peter Morris Page – 73

question: Which virus can cause ureteral stenosis due to ureteritis in transplant patients?

solution.explanation: Answer c – C Polyomavirus (BK virus) can also lead to ureteral stenosis due to ureteritis. Peter Morris Page – 490

question: Which urologic malignancy shows the largest increase in risk after renal transplantation?
options: Renal cell carcinoma of native kidney

solution.explanation: Answer e – The largest increase is seen with renal cell carcinoma (RCC), which more commonly arises in the native kidneys, in part because of the increased risk conferred by acquired renal cystic disease on prolonged dialysis. Radical nephrectomy is performed for tumors of the native kidneys, and nephron-sparing surgery should be attempted for masses in the allograft. Although the risk of RCC is increased most significantly, with up to 15-fold risk over non-ESRD/transplanted individuals, prostate cancer remains the most common malignancy. Peter Morris Page – 493

question: A 24-French (Fr) Foley balloon catheter:
options: can hold 24 mL of fluid in the retainment balloon.

solution.explanation: Answer b – Measures 8 mm in outer diameter. The French or Charrière scale was introduced by Joseph E. B. Charrière as a measurement unit for the circumference of a catheter. One unit on the scale equals 0.33 mm in external diameter. A 24-Fr catheter is therefore 8 mm in outer diameter.

question: Which of the following statements about the healthy adult male urethra is TRUE?
options: The external meatus is the narrowest and should allow a 24-Fr catheter to pass.
The bladder neck is the narrowest and should allow for a 24-Fr catheter to pass.
The prostatic urethra is the narrowest and should allow for a 24-Fr catheter to pass.
The prostatic urethra is the widest and should allow for a 24-Fr catheter to pass.
The external meatus is the widest and should allow for a 32-Fr catheter to pass.

solution.explanation: Answer a – The external meatus is the narrowest and should allow a 24-Fr catheter to pass. The caliber of the urethra varies through-out its course. The normal healthy external meatus should allow for a 24-Fr catheter to pass. Subsequent portions of the adult urethra have a larger caliber, the largest being the prostatic urethra with a caliber of approximately 32 Fr. The bladder neck should be large enough to allow for passage of a 28-Fr catheter

question: Following percutaneous renal surgery, loss of renal function is:
options: approximately 5% of ipsilateral function per access site.
minimal in the absence of vascular injury.
greater than after shock wave lithotripsy.
less in pelvic compared to orthotopic kidneys.
greater in solitary compared to non-solitary kidneys.

solution.explanation: Answer b – Minimal in the absence of vascular injury. The kidney suffers little permanent damage after uncomplicated percutaneous renal surgery. If there is significant loss of function, it is usually owing to disastrous vascular injury or the angioembolization used to treat hemorrhage. Loss of renal function associated with percutaneous renal surgery is less than or equal to the loss associated with shock wave lithotripsy. There is no evidence that damage to the kidney is any more or less in pelvic, orthotopic, solitary, or nonsolitary kidneys.

question: What is the embryologic origin of the seminal vesicles?
options: Swelling of the distal paramesonephric duct

solution.explanation: Answer c – Distal mesonephric duct. The seminal vesicle develops as a dorsolateral bulbous swelling of the distal mesonephric duct at approximately 12 fetal weeks.

question: Which of the following statements regarding renal tubular acidosis (RTA) is FALSE?
options: The hallmark of RTA type I is a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with a high urinary pH (>5.5) in the presence of persistently low serum HCO 3.
Type I RTA is also called distal RTA.
Type II RTA is more common in children.
The hallmark of type IV RTA is hypokalemia.
The form of RTA most commonly associated with renal calculi is type I.

solution.explanation: Answer d – The hallmark of type IV RTA is hypokalemia. RTA type IV is most commonly associated with hyperkalemia. Aldosterone deficiency or resistance leads to decreased secretion of potassium in the distal tubule.

question: The serum urine prostate cancer biomarker PCA-3 represents a:
options: noncoding gene in the TP53 cluster.
noncoding mRNA with no known protein product.
glycosylated protein of molecular weight 60 kD.

solution.explanation: Answer c – Noncoding mRNA with no known protein product. Using differential display and Northern blot analysis to compare normal and prostate cancer tissue, investigators identified the PCA3 prostate-specific gene on chromosome 9q21-22. Study of this gene has determined that it may function as noncoding mRNA, because it has been found to be alternatively spliced, contains a high density of stop codons, and lacks an open reading frame.

question: A 34-week-old female fetus has evidence of normal amniotic fluid and unilateral upper pole hydroureteronephrosis with no evidence of an intravesical ureterocele. What does this most likely represent?

solution.explanation: Answer c – Obstructed ectopic ureter. A duplication anomaly with upper pole hydroureteronephrosis is typically associated with a ureterocele, an ectopic ureterocele, or an ectopic ureter causing obstruction. A dilated ureter is typically identified.

question: Bilateral renal agenesis (BRA) is associated with mutations of:

solution.explanation: Answer c – RET. The association between abnormal kidney development and mutations of RET, GDNF, and GFRα1 in 29 stillborn fetuses with BRA or unilateral renal agenesis. Mutations in RET were found in 7 of 19 fetuses with BRA and 2 of 10 fetuses with URA. A mutation in GDNF was found in only 1 fetus with URA who also had mutations in RET. No GFRa1 mutations were observed. These data suggest that congenital renal agenesis results from RET mutations that prevent or impede the embryonic development of RET-dependent structures.

question: A 5-year-old boy is seen in the office with complaints of intermittent right flank pain. There have been no episodes of nausea, vomiting, or fevers. He has 3 + blood on a urine dip. His physical exam reveals some mild right costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness. Which imaging modality should be used first?

solution.explanation: Answer c – Ultrasound has a more limited role in the assessment of urolithiasis compared with CT but has the distinct advantage of no associated ionizing radiation. Therefore, ultrasound should be considered as a screening tool in the workup for nonemergent abdominal or flank pain.

question: During male reproductive tract development, androgens mediate the differentiation of all of the following structures EXCEPT:

solution.explanation: Answer b – Ureter. Androgens (testosterone, dihydrotestosterone) mediate the differentiation of the paired wolffian ducts into the seminal vesicles, epididymis, vas deferens, and ejaculatory ducts.

question: Bleeding confined by the tunica vaginalis is termed:

solution.explanation: Answer c – Where bleeding is confined by the tunica vaginalis, a haematocele is said to exist. Intraparenchymal (intratesticular) haemorrhage and bleeding be- neath the parietal layer of the tunica vaginalis will cause the testis to enlarge slightly. The force is usually sufficient to rupture the tunica albuginea and tunica vaginalis, and the seminiferous tubules and blood extrude into the layers of the scrotum. This is a scrotal haematoma. Oxford Handbook of Urology Page 545

question: A 32-year-old man undergoes retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for metastatic testicular cancer. Postoperatively, he develops retrograde ejaculation but no urinary incontinence. What structure was most likely damaged?

solution.explanation: Answer c – Division of the hypogastric plexus of nerves during a retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for metastatic testis tumours results in paralysis of the bladder neck. This is of significance during ejaculation where nor- mally sympathetic activity results in closure of the bladder neck so that the ejaculate is directed distally into the posterior, and then the anterior, urethra. Oxford Handbook of Urology Page 624

question: A man with a history of pelvic fracture has remained continent for years. He later undergoes TURP for LUTS and becomes incontinent. What best explains this outcome?
options: The bladder neck was his only functioning sphincter

solution.explanation: Answer c – During pelvic fracture, the external sphincter and/ or its somatic motor innervation may be damaged, such that it is incompetent and unable to maintain continence of urine. Preservation of bladder neck function (the sympathetic innervation of the bladder neck usually remains intact) can preserve continence. However, if in later life, the patient undergoes TurP or BNI for symptomatic prostatic obstruction, they may well be rendered incontinent because their one remaining sphincter mechanism (the bladder neck) will be divided during these operations. Oxford Handbook of Urology Page 624

question: During bladder filling, which stimulus is primarily detected by bladder wall receptors?

solution.explanation: Answer d – Receptors located in the bladder wall sense increasing tension as the bladder fills (rather than stretch). This information is relayed by afferent neurons to the dorsal horn of the sacral cord. Neurons project from here to the periaqueductal grey matter (PAG) in the pons. The PAG is thus informed about the state of bladder filling. The PAG and other areas of the brain (limbic system orbitofrontal cortex) input into the pon- tine micturition centre (PMC) and determine whether it is appropriate to start micturition. Oxford Handbook of Urology Page 626

question: Relaxation of the external urethral sphincter during micturition occurs because the PMC:

solution.explanation: Answer c – The PMC inhibits the somatic motoneurons located in Onuf ’s nucleus (the activation of which causes external sphincter contraction) by exciting gamma- aminobutyric acid (GABA) and glycine- containing inhibitory neurons in the intermediolateral cell column of the sacral cord, which, in turn, project to the motoneurons in Onuf ’s nucleus. In this way, the PMC relaxes the external sphincter. Oxford Handbook of Urology Page 626

question: A 26-year-old primigravida at 12 weeks’ gestation attends for routine antenatal care. She is asymptomatic. Midstream urine culture grows E. coli 10⁵ CFU/mL. What is the most appropriate management?

solution.explanation: Answer c – Asymptomatic bacteriuria Describes an asymptomatic UTI which affects 5– 10% of pregnant women. In the non-pregnant patient, it is defined as two consecutive voided cultures with ≥105 CFUs of the same bacteria, or a single catheterized urine specimen with ≥102 CFUs of one bacterium. However, in pregnant women, treat the infection at the time of the first positive urine culture [rather than wait for a second to confirm asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB)]. If untreated, there is a 20– 40% risk of developing pyelonephritis. NICE guidance recommends routine screening by MSU culture; treatment of ASB reduces the risk of pyelonephritis. Oxford Handbook of Urology Page 660

question: A patient with acute tubular injury has impaired sensing at the macula densa. Which autoregulatory mechanism is most directly affected?

solution.explanation: Answer c – Tubuloglomerular feedback: the flow rate of tubular fluid is sensed at the macula densa of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (Jga), and, in some way, this controls flow through the glomerulus to which the Jga is opposed. Oxford Handbook of Urology Page 835

question: A 58-year-old man with chronic kidney disease develops hyperkalaemia after starting a high-potassium diet. Which nephron segment is primarily responsible for potassium secretion in K⁺ excess?

solution.explanation: Answer d – The majority of K+ is reabsorbed in the PCT. The DCT can both re- absorb K+ in cases of K+ depletion- hypokalemia- (intercalated cells) and secrete it when there is K+ excess (principal cells). It is also secreted by the CD. Overall, the kidney excretes up to 95% of K+ ingested in the diet. Oxford Handbook of Urology Page 837

question: A 62-year-old man with LUTS due to BPH is started on finasteride. Which enzyme is primarily inhibited to reduce prostatic DHT levels?

solution.explanation: Answer b – There are two isoforms of 5AR— type I or ‘extraprostatic’ 5AR (which is absent in prostatic tissue and present in, for example, the skin and liver) and type II or ‘prostatic’ 5AR (which is found exclusively on the nuclear membrane of stromal cells, but not within prostatic epithelial cells). Type I 5AR is not inhibited by finasteride, whereas type II 5AR is. Dutasteride inhibits both type I and II 5AR. Finasteride reduces serum DHT by about 70%, and dutasteride by about 95%. Finasteride re- duces prostatic DHT (type II) by about 80%, and dutasteride by about 94%. We do not know whether these differences translate into differences in clinical efficacy, since neither drug has been compared against the other. Oxford Handbook of Urology Page 72
